doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Tonight Show rehearsals, Mottola and Haggart, Al Klink
summary: Call times, the band's habits, a bass player Mottola silently dismissed, and Al Klink's Miller band sound.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Right. They would have been shocked if he said it swung. You must have had circumstances on The Tonight Show where questionable talent as far as singers and so forth.

Oh horrendous. We didn’t rehearse. We showed up. We had a call, I think we started taping at that time around seven o’clock in the evening. We tried to get going about then. And we had a five o’clock call. And a five o’clock call generally meant that I would check if everybody was going to show up. Because Doc was starting to spread his wares with high school — you know he’d go to, what do you call it—

Clinics. He was suddenly discovering that world. And Rosengarden was always recording someplace, he was always twenty minutes late, and Haggart didn’t want to be there in the first place, and Tony Mottola and Bucky, all of those guys, they rotated the schedule unto themselves, but half the time they’d forget who was there. But it was probably the best, in my opinion, of this period. If you’re going to say — well it was probably the best organization. And it was their organization. Nobody talked. If you talked to any of the guys they’ll say, “I didn’t talk, I just looked.” Mottola was the looker. Haggart, when Haggart said, “I’ve got to get out of here” a couple of nights “You can’t keep me here five nights, I won’t play five nights, I’m out of here.” So it’s hard to find a bass player that plays time. There are a lot of wonderful bass players, but who plays time? So I brought in a young man, we played one tune, and Mottola sat in front of him, a totally quiet Italian, and we finished this tune, and he was a product of the boppers, the bop school, so he played eight thousand notes. Never played anything on the beat, never,

God forbid, played arpeggios all the time. And we finished this tune and there was silence in 6B, and it was like a Kafka movie where all the — well I think it was thirty seconds, but all this time Mottola took a cloth and cleaned off first his guitar and then put it on the rack and slowly turned around and looked at him. That’s all he did. And we knew it was over, he was gone the next night. But I had many adventures like that. Many. I had Al Klink in that band, who came from the Miller band. He was the, when you talk about the Miller band, there was one reason that that band worked with the octave of the clarinet and the tenor, and in tune. Imitators, in my opinion, Walt Levinsky and I talk about this all the time, the imitators never can understand, if they do they just don’t play enough one nighters to get it together, you know. But the real genius of the Miller band was that octave of the tenor and the clarinet. And Al Klink played so magnificently. And Tommy Newsom were our chief tenor players. What a luxury. I’m so lucky to have had that.
